description_full: FirstService Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, provides residential property management and other essential property services to residential and commercial customers in the United States and Canada. It operates through two segments: FirstService Residential and FirstService Brands. The FirstService Residential segment operates as a full-service property manager and provides a range of ancillary services, including on-site staffing for building engineering and maintenance, full-service amenity management, security, concierge and front desk personnel; proprietary banking and insurance products; and energy conservation and management solutions. This segment serves condominiums, co-operatives, homeowner associations, master-planned communities, active adult and lifestyle communities, and other residential developments governed by common interest or multi-unit residential community associations. Its FirstService Brands segment offers property services to residential and commercial customers in North America through company-owned operations and franchise systems under the First Onsite Property Restoration, Paul Davis Restoration, Roofing Corp of America, Century Fire Protection, California Closets, CertaPro Painters, Floor Coverings International, and Pillar to Post Home Inspectors brands. This segment also provides light restoration services, including full-service water, fire and mold cleanup, construction rebuild, and restoration services; painting services; custom-designed and installed closet and home storage solutions; home inspection services; and floor covering design and installation services. FirstService Corporation was incorporated in 1988 and is headquartered in Toronto, Canada.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 30K people. Revenue per employee of $183K ranks in the bottom quartile among Real Estate peers, improving at 16%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $11K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $913 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 13× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10).
financial_summary: FirstService Corporation is a mid-cap real estate business with a $6.4B market cap on $5.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years and +16% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 9% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $318M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.07× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.7× net debt/EBITDA.
Shareholder yield is only 0.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 9.8% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 6% operating margin trails the Real Estate median (23%) by 17pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.31x its revenue share).
It accounts for 1.5% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 16% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 8% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 8% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 31% and a beta of 0.87, it moves roughly with the market.
About $26.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 47% in the 2020 crash and 42% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $86.05 (margin of safety -78%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 30%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $57.91 to $130 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Real Estate peers: P/E 47.0 vs 23.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 17% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $179 on average, 17% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 8.5%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.06).
It converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.07x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 6%.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.7x net debt to EBITDA ($154.4M of cash against $1.1B of debt), above the 1.5x gate.
Goodwill makes up 35% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.6% over 3 years, 14.7% over 5 years and 15.8% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 4.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 8% of annual revenue, deferred revenue up 10% and FFO growth of 8.9% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (2.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 9.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 84%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.8% (0.8% in dividends).
The share count has grown 4.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 10 consecutive years, raising it 12.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 30,000 employees, each generates about $183K of revenue, 0.1x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 15.8% a year.
That works out to $11K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (13x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
